## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Probiotics for Gut Health

URL Source: https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/probiotics

Published Time: 2025-03-04T19:20:39+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: a bowl of yogurt next to a bowl and spoon of probiotic capsules](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AdobeStock_814308481-1024x683.jpeg)
Probiotics—whether from food or supplements—are a hot topic of consumer interest. However, would a relatively healthy person benefit from supplementation of probiotics, or is a fiber-rich diet sufficient for cultivating a robust gut microbiome? Learn more about probiotics, and review available research on supplements and health.

## What Are Probiotics?

Probiotics are dubbed the “good gut bugs” that live in our digestive tract. They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes that make up what we call [the gut microbiome](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/microbiome/). Each person’s microbiome is different, influenced by what we eat, our lifestyle habits, our genes, and environment. Although studies have shown that the types and amounts of gut bugs differ between healthy individuals and those with disease, and that many health experts believe that a diversity of bacteria in the colon is beneficial, what a healthy gut microbiome looks like is still unknown, as it would likely vary from person to person.

However, there are known probiotics that live in the human intestine, such as Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium. The [World Health Organization defines probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24912386) as “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host.” [Early research on probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) used nonharmful bacteria to change or replace intestinal microbes in patients who had intestinal disorders or diarrhea.

### What are prebiotics?

Prebiotics consist of non-digestible fermentable carbohydrates that act as food for probiotics. An example is oligofructose naturally found in wheat, onions, banana, garlic, leeks, and chicory root or inulin. The fermentation of prebiotics by gut bacteria may help increase the amount of beneficial bacteria strains in the colon, prevent the growth of potential pathogens, reduce constipation, support healthy immune function, and lower blood cholesterol levels.

### What are synbiotics and postbiotics?

**Synbiotics** are supplements that contain a mix of probiotics and prebiotics, with the intention that the bacterial strains are fed and thrive in the gut. **Postbiotics**are the “waste” made by gut bacteria after digesting prebiotic fibers, which can include beneficial short-chain fatty acids and vitamin K.

These are terms promoted by industry, as they are marketed as supplements alongside probiotics. However, at this time there is little quality scientific evidence supporting the use of prebiotic, symbiotic, and postbiotic supplements to improve health.

## Sources of Probiotics

Probiotics can be found naturally in or added to certain foods and beverages, and are sold as supplements.

### Food sources

Foods that are fermented tend to contain probiotics, such as:

*   [Yogurt](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/food-features/yogurt/)
*   Kefir
*   Sauerkraut
*   Kimchi
*   [Tempeh](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/soy/)

However, to cultivate a robust gut microbiome, rather than adding just these foods to your diet, focus on implementing a long-term dietary pattern rich in various types of fibers from [fruits, vegetables](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/vegetables-and-fruits/), [whole grains](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/whole-grains/), [beans](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/legumes-pulses/), [nuts](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/nuts-for-the-heart/), and seeds that act as prebiotics.

#### **Do all fermented foods contain probiotics?**

![Image 2: a jar of fermented kimchi with chopsticks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/pexels-shkrabaanthony-6823267-1024x811.jpg)

Fermented foods are foods or beverages that are produced with the intentional, controlled growth of microorganisms with the conversion of food components by enzymes. Historically, fermentation was commonly used to preserve foods as it protected the food from contamination by pathogenic bacteria. It also imparts a unique taste and texture to foods created by the specific types of bacteria used. Certain foods like olives are inedible without fermentation that removes bitter compounds. Fermented foods may benefit the gut microbiome, promote the production of short-chain fatty acids, and support a [healthy immune system](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/nutrition-and-immunity/).

Processing of fermented foods, such as by heating, baking, or pasteurization, reduces or kills probiotics. So popular foods like sourdough bread and commercially prepared fermented vegetables like kimchi and sauerkraut do not contain probiotics unless they have been added back (the label may state “contains live and active cultures”). Additionally, the [International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics state](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33398112/) that the term “probiotic” should not be used interchangeably with “fermented foods.” Instead, fermented foods should be labeled as “containing probiotics” only when there is evidence that the live microbes provide health benefits.For example, yogurt is a fermented food but should only be labeled as “containing probiotics” if the bacterial strains used in its production have been shown to provide health benefits.

### Processed foods and probiotics

You may be surprised to see probiotics advertised on packages of chocolate, cookies, juices, and tea as the food industry has cashed in on growing consumer interest in digestive health and probiotic supplements by conveniently including them in common foods and beverages.

Be wary of [ultraprocessed foods](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/processed-foods/) advertising on front of label, “includes probiotics (or prebiotics) to support digestive health.” This addition may create a favorable impression of their nutritional value but does not make brownies and chips suddenly healthful. Manufacturers also tend to choose familiar-sounding bacterial strains that a consumer will recognize and be more likely to purchase.

#### **Are prebiotic sodas good for me?**

![Image 3: Pink soda cans](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AdobeStock_425896481-1024x686.jpeg)

There is overwhelming scientific evidence of the harmful health effects of [soda and sugary drinks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/healthy-drinks/sugary-drinks/). While soda intake has declined, sodas containing prebiotics have surged in popularity, thanks to the inclusion of [a fiber called inulin](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/carbohydrates/fiber/) and growing consumer interest in gut health. Inulin is naturally found in small amounts in fruits and vegetables like bananas, onions, artichokes, and asparagus. But the type found in ultra-processed foods is usually extracted from chicory root and blended into sweet foods like brownies, yogurt, nutrition bars – and now sodas. These sodas are sweetened with sugar but contain much less than traditional sodas per 12-ounces: about 4-5 grams compared with 40 grams in a cola drink. A soda lower in sugar and containing fiber, especially a fiber type that boasts “prebiotics for gut health” is surely attractive to a consumer. However, it is unproven that the small amount of prebiotics in these sodas will truly improve gut health, and drinking more of them daily to potentially achieve gut health also drives up sugar intake. In fact, a [class action lawsuit was filed in 2024](https://www.fooddive.com/news/poppi-lawsuit-turns-attention-scrutiny-prebiotic-beverage-industry/720066/) against one of these soda manufacturers due to false health claims.

The best use for these prebiotic sodas might be to replace a traditional soda if you’re trying to wean down and lower sugar intake. But they should not be viewed as a health beverage, and remember that the more you drink, the sugar will add up. Check out [Healthy Drinks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/healthy-drinks/sugary-drinks/) for best beverage options.

### Supplements

In 2013, global sales of probiotic supplements was $32 billion, and is [predicted to reach $85 billion by 2027](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/).

In 2020, the International Scientific Association of Probiotics and Prebiotics expanded the definition of probiotics marketed as supplements to include their genus, species, strain, alphanumeric strain designation, and commercial name. For example:

*   **Genus:**_Lacticaseibacillus_
*   **Species:**_rhamnosus_
*   **Strain designation:**_GG_
*   **International strain depository designation:**_ATCC 53103_
*   **Strain nickname:**_LGG_
*   **Product name:**_Culturelle†_

#### **Quality of supplements**

The [supplement industry](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/dietary-supplements/) as a whole is fraught with uncertainties: the quality of products from different sources can vary, and supplement manufacturers do not always have quality control programs in place. Sometimes a probiotic supplement contains lower than the stated dose of bacterial strains or may even contain different types of strains than are listed.

The quality of probiotic supplements depends on the manufacturer. [Important factors include](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) an assurance of potency (ensuring live bacteria in the amounts listed, typically in colony-forming units [CFU] through the end of shelf-life), purity (manufacturing processes that reduce the introduction of harmful pathogens), and identity (current nomenclature used to specify the genus, species, and subspecies, if applicable, and a strain designation for each strain in the product). Live probiotics are susceptible to dying during storage, which manufacturers account for when listing the potency and CFU. Responsible manufacturers will include the dose expected at the use-by date.

## Probiotics and Your Health

There is tremendous interest in the use of probiotic supplements to treat various health conditions or for boosting immunity. As a consumer, you may see attractive claims of health benefits on supplement labels, but be wary as good-quality scientific evidence is still limited and conflicting as to which strains benefit which health conditions, effective doses, single versus multi-strain types, and an optimal length of time to use them. It can be difficult to disentangle scientific evidence from enticing marketing claims.

Probiotic supplements are backed by a billion-dollar industry that often funds published research that shows positive findings about their specific bacterial strain(s). Even if studies, particularly meta-analyses, do not show author disclosures of conflicts of interest, this does not guarantee there are not embedded financial ties. Do not be surprised if your physician or health care practitioner does not recommend probiotic supplements, which is based on low-quality evidence on their efficacy.

Due to lack of high-quality evidence and a largely unregulated supplement industry, buyer beware should be heeded. The [American Gastroenterological Association released practice guidelines in 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/) on probiotic supplements to manage gastrointestinal disorders, and concluded only a few conditions in which they may benefit.They determined that drawing conclusions on probiotic research is difficult due to studies including different strains of microbes used, different doses, and different routes of administration, as well as differences in how the study was conducted and including only small numbers of patients followed for short periods.

That said, research is ongoing and some people find benefit in taking probiotic supplements for specific conditions in the short-term. Multi-strain types (more than one bacterial strain in the supplement) have not necessarily been found more effective than single-strain types. The following conditions have shown low-quality evidence for probiotic use:

*   [Severe diarrhea caused by _C. difficile_ bacterial infections](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/)
*   [Diarrhea from antibiotic use](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29023420/)
*   [Infectious diarrhea in children](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21069673/)
*   [Irritable bowel syndrome](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Probiotics-HealthProfessional/#h7)
*   [Constipation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/)
*   [Ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease only used in a clinical trial setting](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/); [prevention of recurrent pouchitis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38128971/) (an inflammatory condition that occurs after a surgery performed to treat ulcerative colitis)
*   [Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39118769/)

### Are probiotic supplements safe?

As a rule, always discuss supplement use, including probiotics, with your doctor.

There are several species of microbes such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium that are naturally found in the human colon and considered to be safe (not pathogenic). However, people who have weakened immune systems, are taking immunosuppressant drugs, or have severe disease conditions should not use probiotic supplements, because in specific cases they have been [associated with harmful overgrowth or led to health complications](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Probiotics-HealthProfessional/#h15).

## Bottom Line

Probiotics have skyrocketed in consumer popularity. However, there is often industry funding for probiotic research, which can skew results in favor of using the supplements. Despite the hype, there exists mostly low-quality evidence for probiotic supplements. A relatively healthy person would not likely benefit from their use, and those with weakened immune systems should avoid them.

Research is ongoing, and the decision to use supplements should be preceded with caution, with an awareness that there is a level of “manufactured importance” created by industry. General recommendations for probiotics cannot be made, and people should not use them loosely, because each person’s gut microbiome is unique with different bacterial strains that are optimal for them.

Because the safety and effectiveness of probiotic supplements is unclear, the [World Gastroenterology Organisation recommends](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) that if clinicians advise probiotic supplements to patients, the strains, doses, and length of use should only be that of those used in human trials that were shown to be beneficial.However, most consumers and doctors [do not have access to or the ability](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33307023/) to sort through probiotics research, to be able to differentiate among various probiotics products.

A safer natural way to [cultivate a healthy gut microbiome](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/microbiome/) is to implement a dietary pattern that includes a variety of fiber-rich fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes that will “feed” favorable gut bugs. This can include fermented foods that naturally contain probiotics.

## What Are Probiotics?

Probiotics are dubbed the “good gut bugs” that live in our digestive tract. They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes that make up what we call [the gut microbiome](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/microbiome/). Each person’s microbiome is different, influenced by what we eat, our lifestyle habits, our genes, and environment. Although studies have shown that the types and amounts of gut bugs differ between healthy individuals and those with disease, and that many health experts believe that a diversity of bacteria in the colon is beneficial, what a healthy gut microbiome looks like is still unknown, as it would likely vary from person to person.

However, there are known probiotics that live in the human intestine, such as Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium. The [World Health Organization defines probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24912386) as “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host.” [Early research on probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) used nonharmful bacteria to change or replace intestinal microbes in patients who had intestinal disorders or diarrhea.

### What are prebiotics?

Prebiotics consist of non-digestible fermentable carbohydrates that act as food for probiotics. An example is oligofructose naturally found in wheat, onions, banana, garlic, leeks, and chicory root or inulin. The fermentation of prebiotics by gut bacteria may help increase the amount of beneficial bacteria strains in the colon, prevent the growth of potential pathogens, reduce constipation, support healthy immune function, and lower blood cholesterol levels.

### What are synbiotics and postbiotics?

**Synbiotics** are supplements that contain a mix of probiotics and prebiotics, with the intention that the bacterial strains are fed and thrive in the gut. **Postbiotics**are the “waste” made by gut bacteria after digesting prebiotic fibers, which can include beneficial short-chain fatty acids and vitamin K.

These are terms promoted by industry, as they are marketed as supplements alongside probiotics. However, at this time there is little quality scientific evidence supporting the use of prebiotic, symbiotic, and postbiotic supplements to improve health.

### Food sources

Foods that are fermented tend to contain probiotics, such as:

*   [Yogurt](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/food-features/yogurt/)
*   Kefir
*   Sauerkraut
*   Kimchi
*   [Tempeh](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/soy/)

However, to cultivate a robust gut microbiome, rather than adding just these foods to your diet, focus on implementing a long-term dietary pattern rich in various types of fibers from [fruits, vegetables](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/vegetables-and-fruits/), [whole grains](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/whole-grains/), [beans](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/legumes-pulses/), [nuts](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/nuts-for-the-heart/), and seeds that act as prebiotics.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Probiotics for Gut Health

URL Source: https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/probiotics

Published Time: 2025-03-04T19:20:39+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: a bowl of yogurt next to a bowl and spoon of probiotic capsules](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AdobeStock_814308481-1024x683.jpeg)
Probiotics—whether from food or supplements—are a hot topic of consumer interest. However, would a relatively healthy person benefit from supplementation of probiotics, or is a fiber-rich diet sufficient for cultivating a robust gut microbiome? Learn more about probiotics, and review available research on supplements and health.

## What Are Probiotics?

Probiotics are dubbed the “good gut bugs” that live in our digestive tract. They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes that make up what we call [the gut microbiome](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/microbiome/). Each person’s microbiome is different, influenced by what we eat, our lifestyle habits, our genes, and environment. Although studies have shown that the types and amounts of gut bugs differ between healthy individuals and those with disease, and that many health experts believe that a diversity of bacteria in the colon is beneficial, what a healthy gut microbiome looks like is still unknown, as it would likely vary from person to person.

However, there are known probiotics that live in the human intestine, such as Lactobacillus, Bacteroides, and Bifidobacterium. The [World Health Organization defines probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24912386) as “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host.” [Early research on probiotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) used nonharmful bacteria to change or replace intestinal microbes in patients who had intestinal disorders or diarrhea.

### What are prebiotics?

Prebiotics consist of non-digestible fermentable carbohydrates that act as food for probiotics. An example is oligofructose naturally found in wheat, onions, banana, garlic, leeks, and chicory root or inulin. The fermentation of prebiotics by gut bacteria may help increase the amount of beneficial bacteria strains in the colon, prevent the growth of potential pathogens, reduce constipation, support healthy immune function, and lower blood cholesterol levels.

### What are synbiotics and postbiotics?

**Synbiotics** are supplements that contain a mix of probiotics and prebiotics, with the intention that the bacterial strains are fed and thrive in the gut. **Postbiotics**are the “waste” made by gut bacteria after digesting prebiotic fibers, which can include beneficial short-chain fatty acids and vitamin K.

These are terms promoted by industry, as they are marketed as supplements alongside probiotics. However, at this time there is little quality scientific evidence supporting the use of prebiotic, symbiotic, and postbiotic supplements to improve health.

## Sources of Probiotics

Probiotics can be found naturally in or added to certain foods and beverages, and are sold as supplements.

### Food sources

Foods that are fermented tend to contain probiotics, such as:

*   [Yogurt](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/food-features/yogurt/)
*   Kefir
*   Sauerkraut
*   Kimchi
*   [Tempeh](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/soy/)

However, to cultivate a robust gut microbiome, rather than adding just these foods to your diet, focus on implementing a long-term dietary pattern rich in various types of fibers from [fruits, vegetables](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/vegetables-and-fruits/), [whole grains](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/whole-grains/), [beans](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/legumes-pulses/), [nuts](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/nuts-for-the-heart/), and seeds that act as prebiotics.

#### **Do all fermented foods contain probiotics?**

![Image 2: a jar of fermented kimchi with chopsticks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/pexels-shkrabaanthony-6823267-1024x811.jpg)

Fermented foods are foods or beverages that are produced with the intentional, controlled growth of microorganisms with the conversion of food components by enzymes. Historically, fermentation was commonly used to preserve foods as it protected the food from contamination by pathogenic bacteria. It also imparts a unique taste and texture to foods created by the specific types of bacteria used. Certain foods like olives are inedible without fermentation that removes bitter compounds. Fermented foods may benefit the gut microbiome, promote the production of short-chain fatty acids, and support a [healthy immune system](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/nutrition-and-immunity/).

Processing of fermented foods, such as by heating, baking, or pasteurization, reduces or kills probiotics. So popular foods like sourdough bread and commercially prepared fermented vegetables like kimchi and sauerkraut do not contain probiotics unless they have been added back (the label may state “contains live and active cultures”). Additionally, the [International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics state](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33398112/) that the term “probiotic” should not be used interchangeably with “fermented foods.” Instead, fermented foods should be labeled as “containing probiotics” only when there is evidence that the live microbes provide health benefits.For example, yogurt is a fermented food but should only be labeled as “containing probiotics” if the bacterial strains used in its production have been shown to provide health benefits.

### Processed foods and probiotics

You may be surprised to see probiotics advertised on packages of chocolate, cookies, juices, and tea as the food industry has cashed in on growing consumer interest in digestive health and probiotic supplements by conveniently including them in common foods and beverages.

Be wary of [ultraprocessed foods](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/processed-foods/) advertising on front of label, “includes probiotics (or prebiotics) to support digestive health.” This addition may create a favorable impression of their nutritional value but does not make brownies and chips suddenly healthful. Manufacturers also tend to choose familiar-sounding bacterial strains that a consumer will recognize and be more likely to purchase.

#### **Are prebiotic sodas good for me?**

![Image 3: Pink soda cans](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AdobeStock_425896481-1024x686.jpeg)

There is overwhelming scientific evidence of the harmful health effects of [soda and sugary drinks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/healthy-drinks/sugary-drinks/). While soda intake has declined, sodas containing prebiotics have surged in popularity, thanks to the inclusion of [a fiber called inulin](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/carbohydrates/fiber/) and growing consumer interest in gut health. Inulin is naturally found in small amounts in fruits and vegetables like bananas, onions, artichokes, and asparagus. But the type found in ultra-processed foods is usually extracted from chicory root and blended into sweet foods like brownies, yogurt, nutrition bars – and now sodas. These sodas are sweetened with sugar but contain much less than traditional sodas per 12-ounces: about 4-5 grams compared with 40 grams in a cola drink. A soda lower in sugar and containing fiber, especially a fiber type that boasts “prebiotics for gut health” is surely attractive to a consumer. However, it is unproven that the small amount of prebiotics in these sodas will truly improve gut health, and drinking more of them daily to potentially achieve gut health also drives up sugar intake. In fact, a [class action lawsuit was filed in 2024](https://www.fooddive.com/news/poppi-lawsuit-turns-attention-scrutiny-prebiotic-beverage-industry/720066/) against one of these soda manufacturers due to false health claims.

The best use for these prebiotic sodas might be to replace a traditional soda if you’re trying to wean down and lower sugar intake. But they should not be viewed as a health beverage, and remember that the more you drink, the sugar will add up. Check out [Healthy Drinks](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/healthy-drinks/sugary-drinks/) for best beverage options.

### Supplements

In 2013, global sales of probiotic supplements was $32 billion, and is [predicted to reach $85 billion by 2027](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/).

In 2020, the International Scientific Association of Probiotics and Prebiotics expanded the definition of probiotics marketed as supplements to include their genus, species, strain, alphanumeric strain designation, and commercial name. For example:

*   **Genus:**_Lacticaseibacillus_
*   **Species:**_rhamnosus_
*   **Strain designation:**_GG_
*   **International strain depository designation:**_ATCC 53103_
*   **Strain nickname:**_LGG_
*   **Product name:**_Culturelle†_

_†The inclusion of this brand-name is for reference only and does not constitute an endorsement. The Nutrition Source does not endorse specific brands._

#### **Quality of supplements**

The [supplement industry](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/dietary-supplements/) as a whole is fraught with uncertainties: the quality of products from different sources can vary, and supplement manufacturers do not always have quality control programs in place. Sometimes a probiotic supplement contains lower than the stated dose of bacterial strains or may even contain different types of strains than are listed.

The quality of probiotic supplements depends on the manufacturer. [Important factors include](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) an assurance of potency (ensuring live bacteria in the amounts listed, typically in colony-forming units [CFU] through the end of shelf-life), purity (manufacturing processes that reduce the introduction of harmful pathogens), and identity (current nomenclature used to specify the genus, species, and subspecies, if applicable, and a strain designation for each strain in the product). Live probiotics are susceptible to dying during storage, which manufacturers account for when listing the potency and CFU. Responsible manufacturers will include the dose expected at the use-by date.

## Probiotics and Your Health

There is tremendous interest in the use of probiotic supplements to treat various health conditions or for boosting immunity. As a consumer, you may see attractive claims of health benefits on supplement labels, but be wary as good-quality scientific evidence is still limited and conflicting as to which strains benefit which health conditions, effective doses, single versus multi-strain types, and an optimal length of time to use them. It can be difficult to disentangle scientific evidence from enticing marketing claims.

Probiotic supplements are backed by a billion-dollar industry that often funds published research that shows positive findings about their specific bacterial strain(s). Even if studies, particularly meta-analyses, do not show author disclosures of conflicts of interest, this does not guarantee there are not embedded financial ties. Do not be surprised if your physician or health care practitioner does not recommend probiotic supplements, which is based on low-quality evidence on their efficacy.

Due to lack of high-quality evidence and a largely unregulated supplement industry, buyer beware should be heeded. The [American Gastroenterological Association released practice guidelines in 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/) on probiotic supplements to manage gastrointestinal disorders, and concluded only a few conditions in which they may benefit.They determined that drawing conclusions on probiotic research is difficult due to studies including different strains of microbes used, different doses, and different routes of administration, as well as differences in how the study was conducted and including only small numbers of patients followed for short periods.

That said, research is ongoing and some people find benefit in taking probiotic supplements for specific conditions in the short-term. Multi-strain types (more than one bacterial strain in the supplement) have not necessarily been found more effective than single-strain types. The following conditions have shown low-quality evidence for probiotic use:

*   [Severe diarrhea caused by _C. difficile_ bacterial infections](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/)
*   [Diarrhea from antibiotic use](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29023420/)
*   [Infectious diarrhea in children](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21069673/)
*   [Irritable bowel syndrome](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Probiotics-HealthProfessional/#h7)
*   [Constipation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/)
*   [Ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease only used in a clinical trial setting](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32531291/); [prevention of recurrent pouchitis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38128971/) (an inflammatory condition that occurs after a surgery performed to treat ulcerative colitis)
*   [Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39118769/)

### Are probiotic supplements safe?

As a rule, always discuss supplement use, including probiotics, with your doctor.

There are several species of microbes such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium that are naturally found in the human colon and considered to be safe (not pathogenic). However, people who have weakened immune systems, are taking immunosuppressant drugs, or have severe disease conditions should not use probiotic supplements, because in specific cases they have been [associated with harmful overgrowth or led to health complications](https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Probiotics-HealthProfessional/#h15).

## Bottom Line

Probiotics have skyrocketed in consumer popularity. However, there is often industry funding for probiotic research, which can skew results in favor of using the supplements. Despite the hype, there exists mostly low-quality evidence for probiotic supplements. A relatively healthy person would not likely benefit from their use, and those with weakened immune systems should avoid them.

Research is ongoing, and the decision to use supplements should be preceded with caution, with an awareness that there is a level of “manufactured importance” created by industry. General recommendations for probiotics cannot be made, and people should not use them loosely, because each person’s gut microbiome is unique with different bacterial strains that are optimal for them.

Because the safety and effectiveness of probiotic supplements is unclear, the [World Gastroenterology Organisation recommends](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885083/) that if clinicians advise probiotic supplements to patients, the strains, doses, and length of use should only be that of those used in human trials that were shown to be beneficial.However, most consumers and doctors [do not have access to or the ability](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33307023/) to sort through probiotics research, to be able to differentiate among various probiotics products.

A safer natural way to [cultivate a healthy gut microbiome](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/microbiome/) is to implement a dietary pattern that includes a variety of fiber-rich fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes that will “feed” favorable gut bugs. This can include fermented foods that naturally contain probiotics.

Since a landmark 2009 study, researchers have known that a common gut bacterium, *Bacteroides fragilis*, drives colon tumor formation, potentially leading to colorectal cancer, by secreting a toxin that damages the lining of the colon. Pathogenic bacteria such as _Fusobacterium nucleatum_, _Escherichia coli_, _Bacteroides fragilis_, _Enterococcus faecalis_, _Clostridium_, and _Desulfovibrios_ produce detrimental metabolites including polyamines, H2S, TMAO, colibactin, secondary bile acids (DCA), and N-nitroso compounds, which contribute to colorectal cancer through DNA damage, inflammation, and signaling pathway activation. Since a landmark 2009 study, researchers have known that a common gut bacterium, *Bacteroides fragilis*, drives colon tumor formation, potentially leading to colorectal cancer, by secreting a toxin that damages the lining of the colon. But until now, the exact mechanism the toxin uses to latch onto those cells remained a mystery.

A multi-institutional team led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine has identified the missing link. The study, published April 22 in *Nature*, reveals that the *B. fragilis* toxin BFT must first bind host receptor claudin-4 before it can cause damage.

“We’ve made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment,” says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. “Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections.”

The discovery, in fact, already led to the development of a molecular decoy that successfully blocked the toxin’s effects in animal models, offering a potential strategy for preventing *B. fragilis* damage to the colon.

*B. fragilis* can be detected in up to 20% of healthy individuals, and has a potent ability to induce colon inflammation and tumor formation. Prior work in Sears’ lab showed that BFT triggers chronic inflammation in the gut by dividing E-cadherin, a protein essential for maintaining the colon’s protective barrier. In their earlier *Nature Medicine* study, Sears and colleagues showed that the action of BFT leads to colon tumor formation. Yet BFT did not appear to directly attach to E-cadherin. Some other, elusive mechanism appeared to be at play.

Identifying that mechanism began with a genomewide CRISPR screen led by Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate in the Sears lab, in collaboration with the lab of Matthew Waldor at Harvard Medical School. By systematically knocking out genes in colon epithelial cells, White and colleagues from Waldor’s lab identified claudin-4 as the link. When White knocked out claudin-4, BFT toxin was unable to bind to the cells, leaving the E-cadherin target untouched.

“It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit,” says White. “That was an exciting moment.”

The identity of the receptor was a surprise, adds Sears, as she and others in the field had long expected the receptor to be a signaling protein, such as a G-coupled protein receptor, which claudin-4 is not. In a literature review, the team could not identify any other toxin that functions this way, as most proteases go straight to their targets rather than binding a separate receptor first.

To confirm that the toxin and the receptor were physically locking together, the Johns Hopkins team partnered with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona. Using biophysical analysis, White and the Barcelona group demonstrated that BFT and claudin-4 form a tight, one-to-one complex in a test tube, providing the first physical evidence of the binding interaction.

The research then moved from the test tube into living systems through a collaboration with the lab of Min Dong at Harvard Medical School. With Kang Wang and colleagues in Dong’s lab, the team evaluated how the toxin behaved in the complex environment of the gut using mouse models.

By creating a decoy claudin-4 — a soluble protein that displayed claudin-4 sequences — the researchers attempted to prevent the toxin from binding colon cells. Indeed, BFT bound to the decoys instead of the receptor. This decoy strategy successfully protected mice from BFT-induced damage.

“This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties,” says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

The researchers note that one piece of the puzzle remains: While the team identified the receptor and proved the binding, the exact experimental structure of the interaction between BFT and claudin-4 has yet to be captured. Current AI modeling tools, such as AlphaFold, were not able to fully resolve the interaction.

# The Gut Microbiota in Intestinal Health and Colorectal Cancer: A Comprehensive Research Report

## 1. Introduction

The human gut microbiota comprises trillions of microorganisms that play a fundamental role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, modulating immune function, and influencing host metabolism. Disruption of this delicate microbial ecosystem—a state termed dysbiosis—has been increasingly linked to chronic intestinal inflammation and the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer (CRC). Conversely, the strategic use of probiotics and prebiotics has emerged as a promising avenue for mitigating inflammation and retarding CRC progression. This report synthesizes current evidence on the predominant types of gut probiotics, the mechanistic role of prebiotics, the pathogenic bacteria of concern and their toxic metabolites, and the practical dietary implications of these findings.

## 2. Predominant Types of Gut Probiotics

Probiotics are defined by the World Health Organization as "live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host." The most common and extensively studied probiotic genera are **Lactobacillus**, **Bifidobacterium**, and **Saccharomyces** (a beneficial yeast). Among these, *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* species are the most widely used in both research and commercial products.

### 2.1. Lactobacillus

Lactobacilli are Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic or microaerophilic rods that naturally inhabit the human gastrointestinal tract, oral cavity, and vagina. Key species include:

- **Lactobacillus acidophilus** – perhaps the best-known probiotic; found naturally in the mouth, gut, and vagina; helps restore microbial balance across multiple body sites.
- **Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)** – one of the most thoroughly researched strains, with documented efficacy in preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea and reducing gastrointestinal discomfort.
- **Lactobacillus casei** – often used in fermented dairy products; supports immune function.
- **Lactobacillus plantarum** – versatile strain found in many fermented plant foods; produces antimicrobial compounds.
- **Lactobacillus reuteri** – known for producing the antimicrobial substance reuterin.

*Lactobacillus* species primarily colonize the small intestine and contribute to lowering luminal pH through lactic acid production, inhibiting pathogen growth, and enhancing mineral bioavailability.

### 2.2. Bifidobacterium

Bifidobacteria are Gram-positive, anaerobic bacteria that dominate the infant gut, especially in breastfed newborns, and remain important throughout life. Key species include:

- **Bifidobacterium longum** – prevalent in the adult colon; associated with immune modulation and pathogen exclusion.
- **Bifidobacterium breve** – common in infants; supports intestinal barrier integrity.
- **Bifidobacterium bifidum** – produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and antimicrobial peptides.
- **Bifidobacterium lactis** (also classified as *B. animalis* subsp. *lactis*) – widely used in commercial probiotics; demonstrates efficacy in relieving constipation and supporting digestive health.
- **Bifidobacterium infantis** – important for the developing infant gut microbiome.

Bifidobacteria primarily work in the large intestine, forming a microbial barrier that protects against undesirable substances and interfering with pathogen adhesion to the intestinal lining.

### 2.3. Other Notable Probiotic Organisms

- **Saccharomyces boulardii** – a non-pathogenic yeast that is resistant to antibiotics; has demonstrated benefit in preventing and treating antibiotic-associated diarrhea and *Clostridioides difficile* infection.
- **Bacillus coagulans** and **Bacillus subtilis** – spore-forming bacteria with high stability; used in many probiotic supplements.
- **Streptococcus thermophilus** – commonly used in yogurt fermentation; produces lactase, aiding lactose digestion.
- **Enterococcus faecium** – used in some probiotic formulations, though its safety profile requires careful evaluation in immunocompromised individuals.

### 2.4. Food Sources of Probiotics

Probiotic-containing foods include:

- **Yogurt** (with live and active cultures)
- **Kefir** – a fermented milk drink containing multiple bacterial and yeast strains
- **Sauerkraut** (unpasteurized)
- **Kimchi** – a Korean fermented vegetable dish
- **Miso** – fermented soybean paste
- **Tempeh** – fermented soybean cake
- **Kombucha** – fermented tea
- **Pickled vegetables** (naturally fermented, not vinegar-pickled)

It is important to note that processing methods such as heating, baking, or pasteurization can kill live microorganisms. Products labeled as "contains live and active cultures" are more likely to provide viable probiotics.

## 3. Prebiotics: Definition and Mechanistic Role

### 3.1. Definition

Prebiotics are defined as "a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit." This definition, updated by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP), expands the original concept beyond carbohydrates to include other substances, and beyond the gut to other body sites. Most prebiotics, however, are non-digestible carbohydrates—primarily dietary fibers and oligosaccharides—that resist digestion in the small intestine and reach the colon intact, where they serve as fermentable substrates for beneficial bacteria.

### 3.2. Mechanisms of Action

The health effects of prebiotics are multifaceted and involve several interrelated mechanisms:

**1. Selective Stimulation of Beneficial Microbes:** Prebiotics are preferentially fermented by health-promoting bacteria such as *Bifidobacterium* and *Lactobacillus*, leading to increased abundance of these genera. This "bifidogenic effect" is the most consistently documented action of prebiotics.

**2. Production of Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs):** Bacterial fermentation of prebiotics yields SCFAs, primarily **acetate, propionate, and butyrate**. Butyrate is of particular importance for colorectal health:
- It serves as the primary energy source for colonocytes (colon epithelial cells).
- It strengthens the intestinal barrier by promoting tight junction integrity.
- It exhibits anti-inflammatory properties by modulating nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
- It induces apoptosis (programmed cell death) in cancerous cells and inhibits cell proliferation.
- It promotes regulatory T-cell differentiation, supporting immune homeostasis.

**3. Reduction of Luminal pH:** The production of organic acids (lactic acid, acetic acid) during fermentation lowers the colonic pH, which inhibits the growth of pH-sensitive pathogenic bacteria such as *Clostridium perfringens* and *Escherichia coli* strains.

**4. Enhanced Mineral Absorption:** SCFAs and the acidification of the colonic lumen increase the solubility of minerals such as calcium, magnesium, and iron, thereby improving their absorption.

**5. Immune Modulation:** Prebiotics and their metabolites influence immune function through multiple pathways, including modulation of toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, enhancement of secretory IgA production, and regulation of cytokine profiles.

**6. Pathogen Exclusion:** Prebiotics can interfere with the adhesion of pathogenic bacteria to the intestinal epithelium by occupying binding sites or by stimulating mucin production, which strengthens the mucus barrier.

### 3.3. Major Types of Prebiotics

| Prebiotic Type | Examples | Food Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Inulin-type fructans | Inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS) | Chicory root, Jerusalem artichoke, garlic, onion, leeks, asparagus, bananas |
| Galactooligosaccharides (GOS) | Trans-galactooligosaccharides | Legumes, human milk (human milk oligosaccharides), some dairy products |
| Resistant starch | Starch that escapes small-intestinal digestion | Cooked and cooled potatoes, green bananas, legumes, whole grains |
| Xylooligosaccharides (XOS) | Xylan-derived oligomers | Fruits, vegetables, bamboo shoots |
| Pectin | Soluble fiber | Apples, citrus fruits, carrots, berries |
| Beta-glucans | Mixed-linkage polysaccharides | Oats, barley, mushrooms |
| Polyphenols | Secondary plant metabolites | Berries, tea, coffee, red wine, dark chocolate, cocoa |

## 4. Pathogenic Gut Bacteria and Their Toxic Metabolites

A growing body of evidence has identified specific pathogenic bacteria that are enriched in the gut microbiota of individuals with CRC. These bacteria promote carcinogenesis through the production of genotoxins, pro-inflammatory metabolites, and other virulence factors.

### 4.1. Fusobacterium nucleatum

*Fusobacterium nucleatum* is a Gram-negative, anaerobic bacterium that has been strongly associated with CRC. Its pathogenic mechanisms include:

- **FadA adhesin:** Binds to E-cadherin on epithelial cells, activating β-catenin signaling and promoting cell proliferation.
- **Fap2 protein:** Mediates immune evasion by inhibiting natural killer (NK) cell and T-cell activity.
- **Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) production:** *F. nucleatum* generates H₂S, a genotoxic gas that induces DNA damage, disrupts the autophagy process, and alters gut microbiota composition, promoting CRC progression.
- **ADP-heptose secretion:** A pro-inflammatory metabolite that upregulates PD-L1 expression, contributing to immune checkpoint activation and potential immunotherapy resistance.
- **Succinate and formate:** Metabolic byproducts that modulate local immune responses, altering immune cell function and polarization.

### 4.2. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF)

*Bacteroides fragilis* is a common commensal, but enterotoxigenic strains (ETBF) that harbor the *bft* gene produce **Bacteroides fragilis toxin (BFT)**, a 20 kDa zinc-dependent metalloprotease. Recent research (2026) has revealed that BFT must first bind to the host receptor claudin-4 before it can cleave E-cadherin, disrupt epithelial barrier integrity, and activate pro-inflammatory pathways (NF-κB, STAT3, Wnt/β-catenin). This cascade leads to:
- Chronic inflammation
- Enhanced epithelial proliferation
- DNA damage
- Promotion of colon tumor formation

ETBF can be detected in up to 20% of healthy individuals, underscoring the importance of host-microbe interactions in determining cancer risk.

### 4.3. pks+ Escherichia coli

Certain strains of *E. coli* (particularly those belonging to the B2 phylogroup) carry a genomic island known as the *pks* island, which encodes the enzymatic machinery to produce **colibactin**. Colibactin is a genotoxic polyketide-nonribosomal peptide that:
- Covalently alkylates DNA, forming DNA adducts and interstrand cross-links.
- Induces double-stranded DNA breaks and ATR-dependent replication stress.
- Leaves a distinct mutational signature found in approximately one in eight colon tumors.
- Promotes cancer stemness, therapy resistance, and immune suppression.

Recent evidence suggests that colibactin-induced DNA changes are more common in younger adults with early-onset bowel cancer, pointing to a possible contributor to the rising incidence of CRC in younger populations.

### 4.4. Clostridioides difficile

*Clostridioides difficile*, well known for causing antibiotic-associated diarrhea, has been identified as a potential driver of colorectal cancer. Its toxin **TcdB** (toxin B) is the primary culprit:
- TcdB induces inflammatory and carcinogenic pathways in colon cells.
- It modulates mucosal immunity and disrupts epithelial barrier function.
- Mouse models show that toxigenic *C. difficile* alone is sufficient to promote colon tumor formation.
- Epidemiological studies have found that individuals with recurrent *C. difficile* positivity have a significantly increased risk of incident colorectal cancer.

### 4.5. Sulfate-Reducing Bacteria (SRB) and Hydrogen Sulfide

Sulfate-reducing bacteria, including **Desulfovibrio**, **Bilophila wadsworthia**, and **Desulfomicrobium** species, metabolize dietary sulfur compounds (inorganic sulfate and organic sulfur from taurine, cysteine, and methionine) to produce **hydrogen sulfide (H₂S)**. H₂S is a genotoxic and pro-inflammatory gas that:
- Induces DNA damage and genomic instability.
- Triggers hyper-proliferation and pro-inflammatory signaling pathways.
- Disrupts colonocyte energy metabolism.
- Is associated with increased risk of CRC, particularly distal CRC.

A "sulfur microbial diet"—high in red and processed meat, low-calorie beverages, and animal fat—promotes the expansion of sulfidogenic bacteria and is associated with an elevated CRC risk (hazard ratio 1.27).

## 5. Dietary Optimization: Translating Research into Daily Choices

The interplay between diet, gut microbiota, and CRC risk offers a powerful opportunity for prevention. The following dietary strategies are supported by robust evidence.

### 5.1. Increase Dietary Fiber and Prebiotic Intake

A high-fiber diet is one of the most effective dietary interventions for reducing CRC risk. The mechanisms include:
- **SCFA production, especially butyrate:** SCFAs provide fuel for colonocytes, strengthen the intestinal barrier, and induce apoptosis in cancer cells.
- **Reduced transit time:** Fiber increases stool bulk and accelerates bowel transit, reducing the duration of exposure of the colonic epithelium to carcinogens.
- **Inhibition of secondary bile acid synthesis:** High-fiber, low-fat diets shift the microbiota toward saccharolytic fermentation, reducing the production of tumor-promoting secondary bile acids.
- **Reduction of TMAO:** Dietary fiber can inhibit intestinal microbial TMA lyase activity, reducing TMAO production.

**Practical recommendations:**
- Aim for **25–35 grams of dietary fiber per day** (most adults consume less than 15 g/day).
- Include a variety of fiber sources: whole grains (oats, barley, quinoa, brown rice), legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), fruits (berries, apples, bananas, pears), vegetables (broccoli, carrots, leafy greens), nuts, and seeds.
- Incorporate prebiotic-rich foods daily: **garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, Jerusalem artichokes, chicory root, bananas, oats, apples, and flaxseeds**.

### 5.2. Include Probiotic and Fermented Foods

Fermented foods can introduce live beneficial microbes to the gut, supporting microbial diversity and competing with pathogenic species.

**Practical recommendations:**
- Consume **yogurt with live and active cultures** (at least 10⁶ CFU/g).
- Include **kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut (unpasteurized), miso, tempeh, and kombucha** in the diet.
- Consider **probiotic supplements** containing *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* species, especially after antibiotic use, but consult a healthcare provider first, as not all products are of equal quality.

### 5.3. Limit Red and Processed Meat

Red and processed meat consumption is a well-established risk factor for CRC. The mechanisms are linked to:
- Heme iron, which catalyzes the formation of N-nitroso compounds (NOCs) in the gut.
- Sulfur-containing amino acids (taurine, cysteine) that fuel H₂S production by SRB.
- High fat content, which stimulates bile acid secretion and secondary bile acid formation.

**Practical recommendations:**
- Limit red meat consumption to **no more than 500 g (cooked weight) per week**.
- Avoid processed meats (bacon, sausages, ham, salami, hot dogs) as much as possible.
- When consuming meat, pair it with high-fiber vegetables to mitigate harmful effects.

### 5.4. Adopt a Mediterranean-Style Diet

The Mediterranean diet, characterized by high intake of fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, olive oil, and fish, with moderate consumption of poultry and dairy, and limited red meat, is consistently associated with:
- Increased microbial diversity and richness.
- Higher abundance of beneficial bacteria (*Bifidobacterium*, *Lactobacillus*, *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*).
- Increased SCFA production.
- Reduced levels of pro-inflammatory bacteria and metabolites.

### 5.5. Avoid the "Sulfur Microbial Diet"

The "sulfur microbial diet" is a pattern characterized by high intake of red meat, processed meat, low-calorie beverages (with artificial sweeteners), and alcohol, which promotes the expansion of sulfidogenic bacteria. Long-term adherence to this dietary pattern is associated with a 27% increased risk of CRC.

**Practical recommendations:**
- Reduce consumption of red and processed meat.
- Limit alcohol intake.
- Choose water, herbal tea, or unsweetened beverages over artificially sweetened drinks.
- Increase intake of plant-based, sulfur-poor foods.

### 5.6. Consider Synbiotics

The combination of probiotics and prebiotics—termed **synbiotics**—may offer synergistic benefits. Prebiotics can improve the survival and colonization of co-administered probiotics, while the probiotics provide additional metabolic and protective functions. Some studies have shown that synbiotic supplementation can reduce the expression of genes involved in carcinogenic pathways and decrease levels of detrimental metabolites.

### 5.7. General Dietary Guidelines for Gut Health

| Food Category | Recommended | Limit/Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Fruits & Vegetables | ≥5 servings/day; variety of colors | — |
| Whole Grains | 3–5 servings/day (oats, quinoa, brown rice, whole wheat) | Refined grains (white bread, white rice, pasta) |
| Legumes | 2–3 servings/week (lentils, beans, chickpeas) | — |
| Fermented Foods | Yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, miso, tempeh | Heated/pasteurized fermented products (no live cultures) |
| Protein | Fish, poultry, plant-based proteins (tofu, legumes) | Red meat (>500 g/week), processed meats (avoid) |
| Fats | Olive oil, avocados, nuts, seeds, fatty fish | Saturated fats, trans fats, fried foods |
| Beverages | Water, green tea, coffee (in moderation) | Sugary drinks, artificially sweetened beverages, excessive alcohol |

## 6. Conclusion

The gut microbiota occupies a central position at the intersection of diet, intestinal health, and colorectal cancer risk. Beneficial bacteria such as *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* species, supported by prebiotic fibers, produce SCFAs that nourish the colon, strengthen the intestinal barrier, and suppress inflammation. Conversely, pathogenic bacteria including *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, enterotoxigenic *Bacteroides fragilis*, *pks+ Escherichia coli*, *Clostridioides difficile*, and sulfate-reducing bacteria produce genotoxic and pro-inflammatory metabolites that drive DNA damage, chronic inflammation, and carcinogenesis.

The evidence strongly supports a dietary pattern centered on high fiber intake, abundant prebiotic-rich plant foods, regular consumption of fermented foods, and limited red and processed meat—a pattern that promotes a resilient, anti-inflammatory gut microbiota. While the field continues to evolve, and the promise of personalized microbiome-based therapies looms on the horizon, the fundamental dietary principles for cultivating a healthy gut ecosystem are already well established.
